title: {{NAME}} and the Egg in the Amber Forest
moral: Small acts of kindness can restore what time and carelessness have broken.

pages.content: The Amber Forest earned its name from the colour of the light within it, a deep, resinous gold that filtered through the canopy of ancient ferns and tree-ferns sixty metres tall, turning everything to the warm shade of old honey. {{NAME}} had followed the map Princess Veridian had pressed into his hand at the palace gate that morning, a map drawn in green ink on what appeared to be a very large leaf. Veridian herself was somewhere ahead, her voice carrying back through the ferns: 'Keep up! Triceratops are slow at this time of year but the young ones are curious and they will follow you for hours!' The fairies were everywhere in the forest, small as sparks, darting between the fern-stems in trails of amber and rose light. One landed on the brim of {{NAME}}'s hat without permission and began rearranging the gold band with strong opinions. 'That is Pip,' called Veridian, without looking back. 'She adjusts things. Don't take it personally.' Above the fern-canopy, something enormous moved.

pages.content: Princess Veridian was not what {{NAME}} had expected from a princess. She wore a jade travelling gown with deep pockets, practical boots caked with forest mud, and carried a notebook nearly as large as her torso, filled with every dinosaur she had ever observed, described in dense, enthusiastic annotations. Her hair was pinned up with what appeared to be a fossilised claw. She was twelve years old and had opinions about everything, delivered with a brisk confidence that reminded {{NAME}} of a very small general. 'Here,' she said, and stopped so suddenly that {{NAME}} nearly walked into her back. On the ground between the roots of an enormous tree-fern, partly covered in silver moss, was an egg. It was larger than {{NAME}}'s head, mottled blue and cream, and it was cracked along one side with a thin, bright line that pulsed faintly with warmth. 'Abandoned,' said Veridian, her voice carefully neutral, but her eyes were soft. Pip the fairy landed on the egg and placed one tiny hand on the cracked line. She looked up at {{NAME}} with enormous, serious eyes. It was the most serious he had ever been looked at by something the size of his thumb.

pages.content: The fairies came in force. Pip whistled, a sound like a ringing glass, and from all directions tiny forms gathered, streaming between the ferns in ribbons of coloured light. A dozen fairies arranged themselves around the egg in a careful ring, their wings beating in a coordinated hum that produced a warmth {{NAME}} could feel on his face from three steps away. Veridian was already consulting her notebook, cross-referencing the egg's markings. 'Triceratops,' she said. 'If this egg goes cold, it won't hatch. The mother was moved on by a river flood three days ago, according to Pip.' Pip confirmed this with a very specific series of gestures that Veridian appeared to understand perfectly. The warm fairy-hum was slowing, though. The fairies were tiring. 'We need more heat,' said Veridian. 'Sustained, even heat, for at least an hour.' {{NAME}} looked around the forest. Then he looked at his pack and at the emergency supply thermos his mother always made him carry. Still full of hot tea. He removed his burgundy jacket, wrapped it around the egg, and wedged the warm thermos against the crack. Small, but it was something. Every fairy in the ring turned to look at him. Pip made a sound that might have been approval.

pages.content: The hour passed like a held breath. {{NAME}} sat with his back to the tree-fern root, keeping his hand against the jacket-wrapped egg to monitor its warmth, while Veridian read quietly from her notebook, not her notes about dinosaurs, but poems, old ones her grandmother had taught her, because she said warmth was warmth and comfort was comfort and she was not too proud to try something she could not explain. The fairies maintained their ring, spelling each other in shifts. Pip never moved from the cracked line. And then the crack widened, and a small dark eye appeared in the gap, and regarded them all with the ancient, unimpressed wisdom that newborns of all species seem to share. The baby Triceratops was the size of a large dog, already steady on its feet, and it pressed its broad nose first to Pip, then to Veridian, then to {{NAME}}'s hand. The touch was warm and deliberate, like a decision. All of the fairies erupted in a great ringing cheer that sent the fern fronds trembling for twenty metres in every direction. Veridian, who held very firm opinions about emotional displays, turned to write in her notebook and nobody mentioned the single tear that dropped onto the page.

pages.content: The baby dinosaur, whom Veridian named Crest in her notebook before she could stop herself, was collected by its mother before sunset, the large Triceratops emerging from the fern-shadows with a rumbling call that shook the ground pleasantly. Crest looked back once at {{NAME}} with those ancient, dark eyes. Then mother and infant disappeared into the golden forest like two ships into a warm sea. {{NAME}} retrieved his jacket, now bearing a small muddy nose-print, which he decided would be kept there permanently. The fairies dispersed by degrees, Pip last, hovering at eye level with {{NAME}} for one long moment before pressing something cool and small into his palm: a single amber crystal, shaped like an egg. He walked home beside Veridian through the golden evening light, their footsteps crunching on the fern-path. She had stopped talking, which was unusual enough that {{NAME}} glanced over. She was smiling, very slightly, the way people smile when something has happened that is too good for words to hold. He felt it too. He turned the amber crystal over in his pocket all the way home. He slept deeply, and in the morning he wondered if Crest was already walking the forest paths and leaving tiny footprints in the mud.
